cards.title: Polynomial kernels for forbidden-minor vertex deletion
cards.formal: Does vertex deletion to exclude any fixed finite family of graph minors admit a polynomial kernel, parameterized by the number of vertices allowed to be deleted? Precisely, for every fixed finite family \(\mathcal F\), is there a deterministic polynomial-time transformation of \((G,k)\) into an equivalent instance \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) of the same \(\mathcal F\)-deletion problem whose total encoding length and parameter are bounded by \((k+1)^{O_{\mathcal F}(1)}\)?
cards.why: Would give a general guarantee that graphs close to a minor-closed class can be reduced efficiently to a polynomial amount of relevant information. It unifies preprocessing questions for vertex cover, feedback vertex set, bounded-width deletion and planarization.
cards.status_note: Read the original minor and kernel definitions and full concluding question; checked the full planar-family theorem, the full 2022 lossy-planarization version and its 2025 journal status, and the 2026 structural theorem and open-status passage. Searches through 12 September 2026 found no resolution for arbitrary fixed families. The deterministic requirement, family-dependent exponent and exact solution-budget parameter are explicit.

progress.text: The source gives kernels for selected forbidden families and asks whether every fixed-family vertex-deletion problem has a polynomial kernel.
The planar-obstruction condition yields a broad polynomial-kernel theorem.
The journal version of lossy planarization gives a constant-factor approximate kernel, preserving the distinction from exact preprocessing.
STACS work extends structural parameterizations while explicitly retaining the general solution-budget question.

sentences: Delete at most a specified number of vertices to eliminate every minor from a fixed finite family.
The question asks for polynomial-time preprocessing to one equivalent instance of polynomial size in that budget.
The polynomial may depend on the forbidden family.
Families containing a planar obstruction are covered, while planarization remains a key open case.
Later lossy and structural-parameter results do not establish the full exact-kernel claim.

cards.definitions:
The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before inputs are supplied; it is not part of the parameterized input. Its members are finite nonempty undirected graphs and may be disconnected. The original source allows parallel edges, as in its two-vertex examples. Use finite undirected loopless multigraphs with all edge copies explicitly listed for the general convention here; simple graphs are included.

A graph \(H\) is a minor of \(G\) if it can be obtained from a subgraph by contracting edges. Contraction identifies their endpoints, removes resulting loops and retains parallel edges. It is not induced-subgraph containment or topological-minor containment.

The input consists of \(G\) and a nonnegative integer \(k\). It is a yes-instance if there is \(S\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|S|\leq k\) such that \(G-S\) contains no member of \(\mathcal F\) as a minor. All vertices have unit deletion cost. There is no planarity, degree, connectivity or sparsity promise on \(G\). The empty forbidden family is trivial and may be omitted. Since every forbidden graph is nonempty, \(k\geq |V(G)|\) is immediately a yes-instance.

A polynomial kernel is a deterministic algorithm that runs in a polynomial in the total binary input length and outputs a single pair \((G^{\prime},k^{\prime})\) for the same fixed family. It must preserve the yes/no answer exactly on every input. There must be constants \(C_{\mathcal F},c_{\mathcal F}\) such that the total bit length of the output and the numerical value \(k'\) are at most \(C_{\mathcal F}(k+1)^{c_{\mathcal F}}\). Vertex labels can be renumbered. Counting only vertices while leaving arbitrarily many explicit parallel edges or a large encoded parameter would not suffice.

The algorithm, its polynomial running-time degree and the output exponent may depend on \(\mathcal F\). The question does not require one exponent that works for all families, nor an effective procedure constructing the kernel algorithm from an arbitrary family description. Such uniformity requirements would strengthen the target.

The parameter is the solution budget \(k\). It is not the size of a supplied vertex cover, a set whose removal leaves bounded treedepth, or another structural parameter. A kernel supplies one smaller equivalent instance, unlike an algorithm querying many small instances. Approximate kernels that lose a constant factor in deletion cost do not satisfy the exact equivalence requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a polynomial kernel for every fixed finite forbidden family in this solution-budget model, allowing family-dependent exponents, or establish that some fixed family does not admit one. A conventional lower bound of the form “a polynomial kernel would imply NP is contained in coNP/poly” must retain that complexity assumption and is a conditional obstruction, not an unconditional separation. Special-family algorithms and approximate or structural-parameter kernels alone do not establish the universal claim.

context_blocks.title: Fixed-parameter tractability does not fix the kernel size
context_blocks.text: The source observes that every fixed-family problem is fixed-parameter tractable. This guarantees preprocessing to a size depending only on the solution budget, but does not guarantee polynomial dependence.

context_blocks.title: Families with a planar obstruction are covered
context_blocks.text: The FOCS 2012 work obtains polynomial kernels when the forbidden family contains a planar graph. The 2026 introduction explains how a later deterministic approximation removes the randomized ingredient from that kernel construction.

context_blocks.title: Planarization is a remaining special case
context_blocks.text: For \(\mathcal F=\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}\), the output after deletion must be planar. Both obstructions are nonplanar, so the preceding theorem does not apply. The later constant-factor approximate kernel does not preserve the exact decision threshold.

context_blocks.title: The 2026 structural theorem keeps an existence premise
context_blocks.text: Theorem 1 transfers an existing solution-size kernel to a different parameterization for connected forbidden families. It does not supply the missing kernel for every family, and its introduction explicitly retains the general and planarization questions.

cards.context:
The source observes that every fixed-family problem is fixed-parameter tractable. This guarantees preprocessing to a size depending only on the solution budget, but does not guarantee polynomial dependence.

The FOCS 2012 work obtains polynomial kernels when the forbidden family contains a planar graph. The 2026 introduction explains how a later deterministic approximation removes the randomized ingredient from that kernel construction.

For \(\mathcal F=\{K_5,K_{3,3}\}\), the output after deletion must be planar. Both obstructions are nonplanar, so the preceding theorem does not apply. The later constant-factor approximate kernel does not preserve the exact decision threshold.

Theorem 1 transfers an existing solution-size kernel to a different parameterization for connected forbidden families. It does not supply the missing kernel for every family, and its introduction explicitly retains the general and planarization questions.

meta.status_scope: No claim of exhaustive open-status verification
methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. Our primary goal is a benchmark of 500 problems. Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
